title: Service-class adapter: token escrow & soft-throttle for tiered access
creator: Ravi Menon
description:
Background: We currently route requests by plan tier (free/paid/enterprise) and fall back to cheaper model variants when capacity is constrained. During peak bursts this has caused noisy neighbour effects where paid customers briefly lose capacity due to aggressive free-tier admission or bulk spike traffic. This ticket proposes a Service-class Adapter (SCA) layer that introduces a token escrow mechanism plus soft-throttle shaping to make per-tenant quota enforcement more predictable while preserving graceful fallbacks and latency SLOs.

Goals:
- Ensure paid and enterprise plans maintain stable latency and availability under cross-tenant bursts.
- Prevent free-tier spikes from causing abrupt demotions for higher tiers.
- Provide a deterministic, explainable admission signal for downstream router and runtime.
- Support controlled fallback to cheaper model variants without violating per-route latency SLOs.

Non-goals:
- Not a billing change; does not alter metering semantics (usage still billed per-token).
- Not a full replacement for plan-level reservation (reserved capacity remains separate).

Design overview:
1) Token escrow: On request admission, the SCA reserves an escrow token bucket per tenant that is decoupled from immediate token drawdown. Each request places an escrow hold proportional to estimated token cost (based on prompt length & model). If the admission completes successfully, the escrow converts to a charge. If the request is rejected/fails fast or gets routed to a non-compatible fallback, the escrow is released. Escrow smoothing window can be tuned per-plan to avoid transient bursts consuming long-lived quota.

2) Soft-throttle shaping: Rather than hard reject when quota headroom falls below threshold, SCA applies graded soft-throttles: (a) latency-aware delay (micro-sleep with jitter), (b) probabilistic admission (tokenized sampling), (c) recommended fallback hint in the routing decision. These operations are reversible and conservative to avoid cascading timeouts.

3) QoS tiers & SLO awareness: SCA uses plan metadata (free/paid/enterprise), tenant SLA flags, and per-route latency SLO objectives to compute admission weights. Enterprise tenants with explicit SLOs receive minimal soft-throttle and expanded escrow buffers; free tier tenants get shorter escrow windows and higher probability to be suggested a cheaper model variant.

4) Fallback matrix: SCA exposes a ranked fallback list for each model family with cost/latency metadata. The router uses this to attempt up to two fallbacks before returning a degraded error to the client. The SCA ensures fallback attempts respect per-request end-to-end latency budgets.

Implementation details:
- Components touched: routing service (router), admission service (new SCA microservice), runtime admission hooks, policy datastore (expand plan metadata schema), console telemetry (cost/latency breakdown).
- Data model: escrow record per request: tenant_id, request_id, estimated_tokens, escrow_amount_usd, created_at, ttl, state (held/converted/released). Escrow TTL default 5s for free, 15s for paid, 60s for enterprise (configurable).
- Algorithms: sliding-window smoothing for escrow consumption to convert bursty instantaneous usage into amortized consumption. Admission scoring is a weighted sum of (remaining_quota_fraction, sla_priority, estimated_latency_headroom, region_affinity). Tunable weights stored in policy datastore and surfaced in the Console.
- API changes: internal router->SCA gRPC call: AdmitRequest {tenant_id, route_params, model_hint, estimated_tokens, deadline_ms}. AdmitReply {decision, escrow_id, suggested_fallbacks, delay_ms}. External API unchanged for customers; hints included in response metadata only for debug/troubleshooting.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): Enable SCA in us-east router cluster for 5% of free-tier traffic. Monitor latency P99, error rates, and escrow conversion ratio. (2 weeks)
- Phase 2: Expand to paid test tenants with adjustable enterprise escrow TTLs and observe impact. Add cost monitoring. (3 weeks)
- Phase 3: Full rollout across regions with per-region weight tuning and automated fallback policy. (2-4 weeks)

Monitoring & observability:
- New Console metrics: escrow_held_count, escrow_conversion_rate, avg_delay_ms_by_tier, fallback_invocations_by_model, refused_admissions_by_tier, end_to_end_latency_by-fallback-path.
- Alerts: P99 latency increase >15% for paid/enterprise vs baseline, fallback_rate for paid > 5% sustained, escrow_release_rate > 30% indicates estimation mismatch.

Testing strategy:
- Synthetic burst tests with traffic generator to validate smoothing and TTLs.
- Chaos test: inject slow runtime responses and ensure SCA releases escrows and does not deadlock requests.
- Regression tests: validate no change to billing metrics and that fallback path retains correctness for structured output and function-calling flows.

Migration notes:
- Policy datastore schema migration to add escrow settings and per-plan ttl/weights. Backfill defaults on startup.
- Feature flag gating for canary and staged rollout.

Documentation & Console UX:
- Add a Console page in rollout controls to show escrow usage by tenant and offer quick-tune sliders for weights/TTLs.
- Update developer docs with accepted failure modes and guidance for clients to handle probabilistic admission delays and recommended fallbacks.
acceptance_criteria: SCA is receiving router AdmitRequest traffic in canary and responds within 1ms median for simple admits
Escrow conversion rate for paid tenants >= 95% under normal load and conversion_drop < 10% during burst smoothing
No more than 5% increase in paid-tenant P99 latency during canary compared to baseline
Fallback attempt chain respects per-request deadline and does not increase overall error rate by >2%
Console surfaces new metrics and we have at least two alert rules configured
